transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because... honestly, I just don't have anything left in the tank. My body feels completely, utterly drained. And I mean, it's not just like I'm a little tired after a long shift at the hospital, you know? I work as a support worker, so I'm used to being on my feet and moving around, but lately, it's like my limbs are made of lead. Just walking from my car in the parking lot to the front door of the clinic today... it felt like I was wading through wet concrete. Every step took this massive amount of effort, and I had to stop and catch my breath twice. And it's not even just physical stuff. Even sitting at the desk at work, just trying to open the EHR system to log a patient's vitals—something I do a hundred times a day—it takes everything I have just to click the mouse and focus on the screen. It's like my brain and my body are just totally depleted, and I can't seem to get any energy back no matter what I do or how much I rest. It's just this heavy, dragging feeling all the time.
Have you noticed that you don't enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you've lost interest in activities you normally like doing?

Honestly, no, not really. I mean... I still care about the stuff I usually care about, you know? Like, me and my buddies from high school, we always play Xbox on Friday nights. Call of Duty, mostly, or sometimes FIFA if we're arguing about who's actually better at it. And I still really want to play. I still think it's fun. When I'm actually sitting there with the headset on, I'm still getting into it, yelling at the screen, laughing when someone messes up. It's not like the fun got sucked out of it or anything. 

And even with my car... I've been trying to fix up this old Honda Civic I bought off my uncle right after graduation. I'm trying to put in a new stereo system and change out the seats and stuff, and I still love looking at car parts online on my phone and planning what I'm gonna do next with it. So the interest is definitely, like, one hundred percent still there. I haven't lost that at all. It's just... like I was saying before, it's the physical energy to actually go out to the cold garage and turn a wrench that's missing right now. But the actual enjoyment? No, that hasn't changed. I still like all the exact same things, and I still want to do them just as much as I did a few months ago. I haven't noticed any drop in that at all, honestly.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the time lately?

Yeah, I have. I really have. It's... it's like, right after all that energy I used to have just completely dropped off and I started feeling so heavy and drained like I was talking about, this other feeling kind of crept in. It's hard to explain, but it's this deep, deep emptiness. Like, I'll be sitting on my bed, staring at the wall, and I just feel completely hollowed out inside. And the hopelessness... man, the hopelessness is heavy. It's there almost every single day, just weighing on my chest. 

I start thinking about my job, you know? I'm 18, I just got out of high school, and getting this support worker job was a huge deal for me. I was so proud. I thought, 'This is it, this is the start of my career in healthcare, I'm going to work my way up, maybe become a nurse eventually.' But now, feeling like this... I sit there and I just think that I've already ruined it. I feel like I've completely messed up my future in healthcare before it even really got off the ground. Because how can I be a nurse, or even keep this support worker job, if I can't even find the strength to get out of bed without feeling like crying? I just feel so sad and down about it all the time, just constantly beating myself up and feeling like there's no point, like I've already failed. It's just this constant, dark cloud hanging over everything I think about my future.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating a lot less or a lot more than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

Yeah, actually... yeah, big time. It’s funny you bring that up, because I was just noticing it the other day when I was getting dressed for a shift. Um, so usually, I’m a pretty big eater, you know? Like, being an 18-year-old guy, I used to eat constantly. At the clinic where I work, they have this really good cafeteria down on the first floor, and I used to always grab, like, a chicken wrap and fries for lunch, maybe a couple of snacks for the break room. 

But lately... man, I just barely want food at all. It’s like my stomach is just completely turned off. I’ll go the whole day and just completely skip lunch. I won’t even walk down to the cafeteria, I just sit there at the desk. And then I get home after being there all day, and you’d think I’d be starving, right? But I just walk right past the kitchen and skip dinner, too. I just don't have the desire to chew or swallow or prepare anything, it's weird. 

And, well, I realized how much it was actually affecting me because of my work clothes. We have to wear these specific navy blue scrubs for the support worker role, and I bought them right when I started the job, so they fit perfectly. But the other morning, I was tying the drawstring on the pants, and I had to pull it so far just to keep them from falling down. The top, too, it was just hanging way looser on my shoulders, like I was wearing someone else's clothes. I'm definitely losing weight without even trying to, just because I'm basically running on nothing but fluids. Like, I’m mostly just drinking coffee from the machine in the break room—partly to try and force myself to get some of that physical energy back that I was talking about, even though the caffeine doesn't even work anymore—and just sipping on water. But actual solid food? Yeah, I'm barely touching it, and it's definitely showing on my scrubs.
Can you think of any activity that used to make you feel really good or excited, where even the thought of doing it now feels completely unappealing or impossible to enjoy?

No, honestly, like I was saying earlier, I really can't think of anything like that. It's not the enjoyment or the excitement that's the problem at all. 

Like, take the Xbox thing I mentioned. Just this past weekend, my buddy Jake texted me about this new update for Call of Duty, right? They added this new map, which is actually like a throwback to this older game we used to play endlessly back in middle school. And the second he texted me about it, I felt that exact same spark of excitement I always get. I was like, "Oh man, I definitely want to check that out." I was sitting there picturing us getting the old squad together, getting on the mics, talking trash, figuring out the new sightlines... all of that. The thought of it was totally appealing. I wanted to do it just as much as I would have a year ago. It's just... when it came time to actually boot up the console and sit up in my gaming chair, I just felt so physically heavy, like my arms were made of lead, you know? But the actual *wanting* to do it? The feeling good about the idea of it? That's still one hundred percent there. 

And it's the exact same deal with the Honda. I was literally just scrolling through eBay last night for like an hour looking at these custom LED taillights. I was comparing prices, reading the reviews, and then I went down this whole rabbit hole watching YouTube tutorials on how to wire them into the existing harness without blowing a fuse—because the wiring on those older 2000s Civics can be a little tricky if you don't know exactly what you're doing, especially if the previous owner messed with it, which my uncle definitely did. But I was getting super into it, taking screenshots on my phone, planning it all out in my head. I still get that exact same rush when I find a good deal or figure out how a part fits together. 

So, no, I really wouldn't say there's anything that feels unappealing or impossible to enjoy now. The excitement is completely still there in my head, it's just my body that won't cooperate with it, if that makes sense. I still love all my usual stuff just as much as I ever did.
How long have you been feeling this way? When did these symptoms start?

Man, how long... it feels like forever, to be honest. But if I really sit down and look at the calendar and trace it all back, it’s been about nine months. Yeah, right around nine months. 

It all started right after that high-energy period I was telling you about earlier. You know, when I was just going and going and felt like I could take on the whole world? Well, when that finally stopped, it wasn't like a slow fade, it was like I hit a literal brick wall at a hundred miles an hour. I just completely crashed. And ever since that crash, for the last nine months, it’s just been this endless stretch of being completely exhausted, feeling that heavy depression, and just carrying around all that guilt I mentioned about messing up my future.

It’s wild to think it’s been that long, almost a whole year, just waking up every single day feeling like I’m dragging a hundred pounds of weights behind me. I keep trying to remember the exact day it switched, like, was I at the clinic? Was I in my room? I just remember the energy literally draining out of my legs, and then this dark cloud just settled over me. And it hasn't lifted once in nine months. Like, not even for a single afternoon. I keep waiting to wake up and feel like myself again, or even just get a fraction of that old energy back so I can actually do my job properly, but it's just been nine solid months of feeling totally hollowed out and guilty about everything. It's just... I don't know, it's a really long time to feel this exhausted, you know? It really wears you down when it goes on for nine months straight.
Before this current period of feeling drained and depressed, have you ever had any other times in your life where you felt down or hopeless for at least a couple of weeks at a time?

Before this? Um... no. No, honestly, I really haven't. I mean, sure, back in high school I’d have a bad day here or there, like if I bombed a test or got into an argument with a buddy, but it was never anything that lasted for weeks at a time. I was always a pretty upbeat guy, you know? Always looking forward to things, always making plans. So this whole thing is completely new to me. 

It really was just... like I was saying, after all that energy dropped, that’s exactly when it started. I just started feeling completely empty and hopeless most days. And it’s this really specific, heavy kind of hopelessness, too. It’s like... like I had already ruined my future in healthcare before it even really started. 

Because getting this support worker job at the clinic, that was a huge deal for me. I’m only eighteen, and most places won't even look at you without more experience or a college degree, but I managed to get my foot in the door. I was planning to use it to network, you know, talk to the nurses, maybe figure out if I wanted to go to nursing school or become a tech or something. It was supposed to be the beginning of my whole life. I had it all mapped out in my head.

But then that crash happened, and that emptiness just moved in and took over everything. I’d be sitting there at the clinic, just staring at the floor, feeling like an absolute fraud. Every single day I wake up with that same heavy, hopeless feeling, just convinced that everyone at the clinic already knows I'm useless now and that I've completely blown my one big chance. I just sit there thinking about how I was supposed to be building this great career, and instead, I can't even function enough to walk down to the cafeteria. So, yeah, to answer your question, I've never felt anything even close to this before. It all just started the second that energy disappeared, and it’s just been this massive, hopeless void ever since.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or so irritable that it was hard to control yourself, even if others didn’t notice it?

Yeah, actually, that's exactly what I was talking about earlier when I mentioned that high-energy period before the crash. It was... man, it was intense. For a while there, I just felt absolutely amazing. Like, completely unstoppable. I’d walk into the clinic for my shift and just feel this buzzing electricity, like I could do the work of five people, no problem. I was moving so fast, getting everything done, just feeling on top of the world, like I was the best hire they'd ever made. 

But the thing is, because I felt so incredible and like my brain was working at lightning speed, I had absolutely zero patience for anyone else. Like, none. If one of the nurses or the shift supervisor came up to me and tried to correct my documentation—because, you know, we have these really specific electronic health record forms we have to fill out for every single patient interaction, and they can be super tedious with all the drop-down menus and checkboxes—if someone even hinted that I missed a box or told me I needed to slow down and be more careful, I would just completely snap at them. 

It was like they were personally insulting me, you know? I’d get so unbelievably irritated, like my blood was boiling instantly, just because they were interrupting my flow. I remember snapping at one of the senior nurses just because she told me to take a breath and double-check a chart before filing it. I basically bit her head off, which is so not like me. I'm usually really respectful, especially since I'm the youngest guy there and trying to learn the ropes. But in those weeks, I just felt so high up and untouchable, and anyone getting in my way or telling me to slow my pace down was just... infuriating. It was this crazy mix of feeling like an absolute superhero but also being a split-second away from exploding if anyone questioned how I was doing my job. So yeah, I definitely had a period exactly like what you're describing.
How long did that high-energy, irritable period last before it switched to the crash and the depression started?

Well, see, the whole thing kind of crept up on me, but if I really look at the timeline... the whole crisis built up over about two months. Yeah, two months. And it's actually really specific why it started then, because it was right after the clinic changed my responsibilities. 

See, when I first started there, I was mostly just doing basic stuff, you know? Greeting patients, walking them back to the rooms, wiping down the exam tables, maybe grabbing extra gauze or whatever the nurses needed. It was busy, but it was straightforward. But then, they had this big staff meeting, and because they were short-staffed—which, honestly, they're always short-staffed, it's a huge problem in healthcare right now—they decided to cross-train some of us support workers to do more administrative stuff. So suddenly, I was the one responsible for initiating the electronic intake forms, verifying insurance codes, and making sure all the preliminary vitals were logged into the system before the doctor even stepped in the room. 

And at first, I was like, "Okay, cool, more responsibility, this is good for my resume." But then... that’s when that energy started kicking in. I started feeling like I could do all the new admin stuff *and* all my old physical tasks, all at the same time, faster than anyone else. I was practically running from the front desk to the exam rooms. And that intense, buzzing, irritable feeling I was telling you about? That whole period where I felt like a superhero but would snap at anyone who looked at me wrong? That lasted for those entire two months. 

It was just this crazy two-month build-up where I was doing the work of three people, feeling like my brain was on fire in the best way possible, but also getting so mad at the nurses if they told me I put the wrong billing code in. I just couldn't handle them slowing me down. So yeah, it was exactly two months of that intense build-up right after they changed my job duties, and then... bam. The brick wall. The crash. And then the nine months of this awful emptiness started. But those two months before the crash, man, they were just wild. I've never moved that fast in my entire life.

It's just... I don't know, it's a really long time to feel this exhausted, you know? It really wears you down when it goes on for nine months straight.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had any previous episodes of depression lasting at least two weeks before the current one, to distinguish between a first episode (F32.3) and recurrent depressive disorder (F33.3).
doctor.question: Before this current period of feeling drained and depressed, have you ever had any other times in your life where you felt down or hopeless for at least a couple of weeks at a time?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: After all that energy dropped, I started feeling empty and hopeless most days, like I had already ruined my future in healthcare before it even really started.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of feeling down or hopeless. This directly maps to the Depressed Mood symptom, allowing the patient to address the question by describing their current feelings of emptiness and hopelessness.

patient.answer:
Before this? Um... no. No, honestly, I really haven't. I mean, sure, back in high school I’d have a bad day here or there, like if I bombed a test or got into an argument with a buddy, but it was never anything that lasted for weeks at a time. I was always a pretty upbeat guy, you know? Always looking forward to things, always making plans. So this whole thing is completely new to me. 

It really was just... like I was saying, after all that energy dropped, that’s exactly when it started. I just started feeling completely empty and hopeless most days. And it’s this really specific, heavy kind of hopelessness, too. It’s like... like I had already ruined my future in healthcare before it even really started. 

Because getting this support worker job at the clinic, that was a huge deal for me. I’m only eighteen, and most places won't even look at you without more experience or a college degree, but I managed to get my foot in the door. I was planning to use it to network, you know, talk to the nurses, maybe figure out if I wanted to go to nursing school or become a tech or something. It was supposed to be the beginning of my whole life. I had it all mapped out in my head.

But then that crash happened, and that emptiness just moved in and took over everything. I’d be sitting there at the clinic, just staring at the floor, feeling like an absolute fraud. Every single day I wake up with that same heavy, hopeless feeling, just convinced that everyone at the clinic already knows I'm useless now and that I've completely blown my one big chance. I just sit there thinking about how I was supposed to be building this great career, and instead, I can't even function enough to walk down to the cafeteria. So, yeah, to answer your question, I've never felt anything even close to this before. It all just started the second that energy disappeared, and it’s just been this massive, hopeless void ever since.

doctor.intent: Ask about the presence of a manic or hypomanic episode to differentiate between F32.3 (Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, Severe) and F33.3 (Bipolar Disorder, Current Episode Depressed, Severe).
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of time where you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or so irritable that it was hard to control yourself, even if others didn’t notice it?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Some days I felt amazing and unstoppable, then if someone corrected my documentation or told me to slow down I would snap at them like they were insulting me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of feeling unusually high, overly energetic, or irritable, which directly corresponds to an elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, that's exactly what I was talking about earlier when I mentioned that high-energy period before the crash. It was... man, it was intense. For a while there, I just felt absolutely amazing. Like, completely unstoppable. I’d walk into the clinic for my shift and just feel this buzzing electricity, like I could do the work of five people, no problem. I was moving so fast, getting everything done, just feeling on top of the world, like I was the best hire they'd ever made. 

But the thing is, because I felt so incredible and like my brain was working at lightning speed, I had absolutely zero patience for anyone else. Like, none. If one of the nurses or the shift supervisor came up to me and tried to correct my documentation—because, you know, we have these really specific electronic health record forms we have to fill out for every single patient interaction, and they can be super tedious with all the drop-down menus and checkboxes—if someone even hinted that I missed a box or told me I needed to slow down and be more careful, I would just completely snap at them. 

It was like they were personally insulting me, you know? I’d get so unbelievably irritated, like my blood was boiling instantly, just because they were interrupting my flow. I remember snapping at one of the senior nurses just because she told me to take a breath and double-check a chart before filing it. I basically bit her head off, which is so not like me. I'm usually really respectful, especially since I'm the youngest guy there and trying to learn the ropes. But in those weeks, I just felt so high up and untouchable, and anyone getting in my way or telling me to slow my pace down was just... infuriating. It was this crazy mix of feeling like an absolute superhero but also being a split-second away from exploding if anyone questioned how I was doing my job. So yeah, I definitely had a period exactly like what you're describing.

inference.note: The patient reported a prior period of abnormally elevated mood and irritability, which introduces Bipolar I Disorder, Current Episode Depressed (F31.3) as a new candidate. The prior candidates (F32.3 and F33.3) remain due to the severity, duration, and persistence of the depressive symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the elevated/irritable mood period to assess for potential bipolar I disorder (F31.3).
doctor.question: How long did that high-energy, irritable period last before it switched to the crash and the depression started?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The whole crisis built up over about two months after my clinic changed my responsibilities.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the duration of the high-energy, irritable period (the manic episode), which corresponds to the 'Duration' item in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, see, the whole thing kind of crept up on me, but if I really look at the timeline... the whole crisis built up over about two months. Yeah, two months. And it's actually really specific why it started then, because it was right after the clinic changed my responsibilities. 

See, when I first started there, I was mostly just doing basic stuff, you know? Greeting patients, walking them back to the rooms, wiping down the exam tables, maybe grabbing extra gauze or whatever the nurses needed. It was busy, but it was straightforward. But then, they had this big staff meeting, and because they were short-staffed—which, honestly, they're always short-staffed, it's a huge problem in healthcare right now—they decided to cross-train some of us support workers to do more administrative stuff. So suddenly, I was the one responsible for initiating the electronic intake forms, verifying insurance codes, and making sure all the preliminary vitals were logged into the system before the doctor even stepped in the room. 

And at first, I was like, "Okay, cool, more responsibility, this is good for my resume." But then... that’s when that energy started kicking in. I started feeling like I could do all the new admin stuff *and* all my old physical tasks, all at the same time, faster than anyone else. I was practically running from the front desk to the exam rooms. And that intense, buzzing, irritable feeling I was telling you about? That whole period where I felt like a superhero but would snap at anyone who looked at me wrong? That lasted for those entire two months. 

It was just this crazy two-month build-up where I was doing the work of three people, feeling like my brain was on fire in the best way possible, but also getting so mad at the nurses if they told me I put the wrong billing code in. I just couldn't handle them slowing me down. So yeah, it was exactly two months of that intense build-up right after they changed my job duties, and then... bam. The brick wall. The crash. And then the nine months of this awful emptiness started. But those two months before the crash, man, they were just wild. I've never moved that fast in my entire life.

inference.note: The patient described a distinct prior period of abnormally elevated mood and increased energy (lasting two months) that meets criteria for a manic episode, followed by a nine-month period of depressive symptoms. This supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder, Current Episode Depressed, Severe, With Psychotic Features (F31.3). The other depressive disorders (F32.3, F33.3) are ruled out because the patient has a clear history of a manic episode, which excludes unipolar depression.
